title: Multiple Files and Headers
summary: Real programs are split across files. A **header** (`.h`) says **what exists**. A **source file** (`.cpp`) says **how it works**. `#include` the header wherever you need those functions.
markdown:
## Why split a program up? A program in one file is fine at fifty lines. At five thousand it is a nightmare to find anything in. So programmers group related functions into their own files. That raises a problem you met in the last lesson: a function must be known before it is called. If `add` lives in another file, how does `main.cpp` know about it? The answer is a **header file**. ## Menu and kitchen Think of a restaurant. The **menu** lists what you can order. The **kitchen** is where the food is made. You only need the menu to order. ```mermaid flowchart LR H["mathx.h
the menu
(declarations)"] C["mathx.cpp
the kitchen
(definitions)"] M["main.cpp
the customer
(calls the functions)"] H -.->|"#include"| C H -.->|"#include"| M ``` | File | Contains | Example | |---|---|---| | `mathx.h` | **Declarations**: the name of each function, what it needs and what it returns | `int add(int x, int y);` | | `mathx.cpp` | **Definitions**: the actual instructions | `int add(int x, int y) { return x + y; }` | | `main.cpp` | Code that **uses** the functions | `add(2, 3)` | ### mathx.h ```cpp #pragma once int add(int x, int y); int multiply(int x, int y); ``` ### mathx.cpp ```cpp #include "mathx.h" int add(int x, int y) { return x + y; } int multiply(int x, int y) { return x * y; } ``` ### main.cpp ```cpp #include #include "mathx.h" int main() { std::cout << add(2, 3) << ' ' << multiply(2, 3) << '\n'; return 0; } ``` In Xenon, tasks with several files show each file as a tab above the editor, and all of them are built together when you press **Run**. ## What `#include` really does Nothing clever. It **pastes** the contents of the named file in at that spot, before the compiler starts. ``` main.cpp as you wrote it main.cpp as the compiler sees it ┌──────────────────────────┐ ┌────────────────────────────┐ │ #include "mathx.h" │ ───▶ │ int add(int x, int y); │ │ │ │ int multiply(int x, int y);│ │ int main() { ... } │ │ int main() { ... } │ └──────────────────────────┘ └────────────────────────────┘ ``` | Written as | Used for | |---|---| | `#include ` | Headers that come with C++ | | `#include "mathx.h"` | Headers you wrote yourself | ## How the pieces are joined Remember the compiler and the linker from the first lesson? This is where the linker earns its place. ```mermaid flowchart TD MC["main.cpp"] -->|"compiled on its own"| MO["main.obj
needs: add, multiply"] XC["mathx.cpp"] -->|"compiled on its own"| XO["mathx.obj
provides: add, multiply"] MO --> L["Linker
matches needs to provides"] XO --> L L --> EXE["program.exe"] ``` Each `.cpp` file is compiled **separately**. While compiling `main.cpp`, the compiler only has the declaration of `add`. It trusts that the real thing exists somewhere. The linker then checks that it does. > [!warning] "Unresolved external symbol" > This is the linker saying: "something calls `add`, but no file provides it." Either you declared a function and never wrote it, or its definition does not match the declaration exactly (a different name or different parameters). ## `#pragma once` Put this as the first line of every header you write. It stops the header being pasted twice into the same file, which can cause "already defined" errors as programs grow. ## One rule to remember | | How many times? | Where it goes | |---|---|---| | **Declaration** (`int add(int x, int y);`) | As often as you like | The header | | **Definition** (the version with a body) | **Exactly once** in the whole program | A `.cpp` file | If you put a function's body in a header, every file that includes it gets its own copy, and the linker complains that it has too many. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What goes in a header file? - The `main` function + Declarations: the functions that exist, without their bodies - The full definitions of every function - Only `#include` lines > A header is the "menu": declarations of what exists. The bodies go in a `.cpp` file, which is compiled once. ? What is the difference between `` and `"mathx.h"` in an `#include`? - Angle brackets are for `.h` files; quotes are for files without an extension - There is none; both forms mean exactly the same + Angle brackets are for headers that come with C++; quotes are for your own files - Quotes include the file once; angle brackets include it every time > Use `<...>` for the standard headers that come with C++ and `"..."` for headers you wrote, which are looked for next to your code first. ? You get "unresolved external symbol add". Is that the compiler or the linker? - The compiler: `add` was never declared + The linker: no file provides the definition of `add` - The compiler: `add` has a typo in its body - Neither; it is a crash while the program runs > The compiler was happy because it saw a declaration. The **linker** then could not find any file that defines `add`. ? What does `#include` actually do? - It links a finished library into the program - It lets the compiler look up names in another file only when needed + It pastes the contents of the named file in at that point before compiling > `#include` is a plain copy and paste, done before the compiler proper sees the code. ```
ideas:
1. Create `greet.h` and `greet.cpp` with a function `void greet(std::string name)`. Call it from `main.cpp`.
2. Change the function's name in `greet.cpp` only. Read the linker error.
3. Add a second function to the pair of files and call that too.

cards.q: What goes in a header file?
cards.a:
Declarations: the functions that exist, without their bodies

A header is the "menu": declarations of what exists. The bodies go in a `.cpp` file, which is compiled once.

cards.q: What is the difference between `<iostream>` and `"mathx.h"` in an `#include`?
cards.a:
Angle brackets are for headers that come with C++; quotes are for your own files

Use `<...>` for the standard headers that come with C++ and `"..."` for headers you wrote, which are looked for next to your code first.

cards.q: You get "unresolved external symbol add". Is that the compiler or the linker?
cards.a:
The linker: no file provides the definition of `add`

The compiler was happy because it saw a declaration. The **linker** then could not find any file that defines `add`.

It pastes the contents of the named file in at that point before compiling

`#include` is a plain copy and paste, done before the compiler proper sees the code.
